title: Right upper quadrant pain, abdominal swelling and vomiting blood
desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of a 62-year-old man with right upper quadrant pain, abdominal swelling and haematemesis after 15 years of heavy drinking that has escalated in the month since his wife died. The candidate then interprets his repeat observations, bloods and abdominal ultrasound, gives the diagnosis and differentials, and outlines emergency management, an explanation to the patient and safety netting.
focus: Haematemesis in a heavy drinker: recognising decompensated alcohol-related liver disease and managing a suspected variceal bleed
stem: You are the junior doctor in the Emergency Department. James Holloway, a 62-year-old retired journalist, has come in with abdominal pain, and he vomited blood this morning. He is in an acute bay with monitoring attached. A nurse is with you, can carry out your instructions and will tell you his observations when you ask.
tasks: Take a focused history from James and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining. Give the nurse any immediate instructions you need to (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you his repeat observations, his blood results and his abdominal ultrasound report. Interpret them, give your most likely diagnosis and differentials, outline your management approach, answer James's question and give safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are James Holloway, a 62-year-old retired journalist. You are pale, a little sweaty and worried. You are a frank man who doesn't hide his drinking once he is asked about it, and you get tearful talking about your wife Margaret. You are fully alert and answer clearly. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they are examining.

Opening line: "I've had this pain under my ribs for ages, but this morning I brought up blood, and that frightened me."

The nurse (give when asked):

  • Observations on arrival: HR 108 regular, BP 118/74 lying, RR 18, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C, BGL 6.2 mmol/L, alert.
  • If the candidate asks for IV access and bloods: "Two large-bore cannulae are in and bloods are sent, including a group and hold." If they ask for crossmatch, nil by mouth or senior notification, the nurse confirms it is done.
  • If the candidate asks for a lying and sitting or standing BP: sitting up, BP 100/64 and HR 124, and James says he feels light-headed. It settles when he lies back.
  • If the candidate orders medicines or other treatment in Part 1, the examiner says: "Noted. Please cover your management in Part 2." If they ask for results, say these will come in Part 2.

History (give only when asked):

The vomiting of blood

  • This morning at about 7 am you vomited twice, about a cupful each time. It was bright red blood with some dark clots. You have never vomited blood before.
  • You were not retching or vomiting before the blood came up. It came up on its own.
  • You had a black, sticky, very smelly bowel motion this morning. Before that your bowels were normal.
  • You felt dizzy when you stood up afterwards but did not faint.

The pain

  • Under the right ribs, just below the rib margin. It doesn't go anywhere else.
  • It came on gradually. It is a dull, throbbing ache.
  • A mild ache (2/10) has been there for about 3 years. Over the past 3 weeks it has got worse, up to 7/10. Today it is 5/10.
  • Bending over makes it worse. Nothing makes it better.
  • It isn't colicky, it isn't related to meals, and it doesn't go through to your back.
  • "I didn't think much of it at first, but it just seems to be getting worse."

Other symptoms

  • Your tummy has been swelling over the past 3 weeks. Your trousers no longer do up.
  • You have been more tired over the past couple of weeks. The pain and the swelling stop you walking the dogs and exercising, and they get in the way of everyday things.
  • No weight loss that you know of (you have got bigger round the middle). Your appetite is a bit less. No night sweats, fevers or chills.
  • You haven't noticed yellow skin or eyes. No pale bowel motions, no dark urine, no itch.
  • No heartburn or indigestion. No pain in the upper middle of the tummy. No pale, greasy or floating bowel motions.
  • No confusion. Your shakes: your hands have been a bit shaky in the mornings lately, and a drink settles them. You have never had a fit, seen things or been treated for withdrawal.

Past history, medicines and allergies

  • High blood pressure for 15 years. High cholesterol for 12 years. Nothing else, no operations, never had a gastroscopy.
  • Perindopril and simvastatin, one tablet of each every day. You usually take them reliably, but this past month you have been forgetting, because Margaret used to remind you.
  • No aspirin, anti-inflammatories, blood thinners, steroids or supplements. You have never been tested for the stomach bug (H. pylori).
  • No allergies.

Hepatitis and other liver risks (only if asked)

  • No injecting drugs ever, no tattoos, no blood transfusions. Married to Margaret for 36 years, no other partners. You have never had a hepatitis test.
  • No diabetes. You were told years ago your weight was "a bit over".

Alcohol

  • For about 15 years: around 5 standard drinks a night on weekdays and about 10 a day on weekends, mostly red wine.
  • In the past month, since Margaret died, about 15 standard drinks a day (nearly 2 bottles of red wine) "to cope".
  • Your last drink was at about 11 pm last night.
  • If asked: "I think it may have something to do with my drinking. I've been drinking quite a bit more in the past month, ever since my wife passed away."

Family history: your mother is 87 and has dementia. Your father died of a heart attack at 82.

Social history

  • Never smoked. No recreational drugs.
  • Margaret died suddenly of a stroke a month ago. You now live alone with your 2 dogs.
  • Your children, aged 35 and 31, live interstate and fly down about once a month.
  • You retired from journalism 12 years ago.
  • Mood (only if asked): you feel very low and lonely and aren't sleeping well. You have no thoughts of harming yourself. "The dogs keep me going."

Ideas, concerns, expectations: you suspect your drinking is behind this and you feel ashamed of it. You are frightened by the blood. You are worried about who will feed the dogs if you have to stay in. You want to know what is going on and whether you will need to stay in hospital.

Question to raise once: "Is this something serious?"

Exam findings (give only for what the candidate examines):

  • General: pale and slightly clammy. Capillary refill 3 seconds centrally. Peripheries cool. Alert and oriented to time, place and person. Slightly yellow sclerae. Thin arms with a swollen abdomen.
  • Hands and arms: palmar erythema on both hands, white nails (leukonychia), no clubbing, no Dupuytren contracture. Several bruises on both forearms. A fine tremor of the outstretched hands. No asterixis.
  • Face and neck: scleral icterus. Conjunctival pallor. No parotid enlargement. JVP not raised.
  • Chest: 6 spider naevi over the upper chest and shoulders. Bilateral gynaecomastia. Heart sounds normal. Chest clear.
  • Abdomen, inspection: distended with full flanks. No caput medusae. No scars.
  • Abdomen, palpation: mild tenderness in the right upper quadrant with no guarding or rebound, Murphy's sign negative. Firm, irregular liver edge 3 cm below the right costal margin. Spleen tip palpable on deep inspiration.
  • Abdomen, percussion and auscultation: dull in both flanks, with shifting dullness present. Bowel sounds normal.
  • Rectal examination (if requested, with a chaperone): black, tarry stool on the glove (melaena). No fresh blood, no mass.
  • Legs: bilateral pitting oedema to mid-shin.
  • Mental state: oriented, can say the months backwards without error, not drowsy.

check.x: Professionalism
Hand hygiene, introduces self, confirms James's identity and gains consent for the history and examination.

Recognises an active upper GI bleed from the start and gives the nurse early instructions before the detailed history: monitoring, two large-bore cannulae, bloods including group and crossmatch, nil by mouth, and senior ED doctor informed.
check.d: Critical elements: two large-bore cannulae, bloods with group and crossmatch (or group and hold with blood made ready), and a senior informed, given before the detailed history. Credit monitoring and nil by mouth but do not require them.

check.x: Asks about alcohol in a non-judgemental way and responds with empathy to the death of his wife.
History
Characterises the haematemesis:

kids.x: Amount, colour and timing: twice this morning, about a cupful each time, bright red blood with clots, the first episode ever
Whether he retched before the blood came up (no retching, which argues against a Mallory-Weiss tear)
Melaena (black, tarry stool this morning) and dizziness or fainting (dizzy on standing, no syncope)

check.x: Characterises the pain: site (right upper quadrant below the costal margin), character (dull, throbbing), duration and recent worsening (2/10 for 3 years, 7/10 over 3 weeks).
Elicits the abdominal swelling over 3 weeks, the fatigue, and their effect on daily activities and exercise.
Takes a quantified alcohol history:

kids.x: Standard drinks over time: about 5 a day on weekdays and 10 on weekend days for 15 years, about 15 a day in the past month since his wife died
Time of last drink (11 pm last night) and withdrawal features: morning shakes relieved by a drink, no previous withdrawal seizures or hallucinations

check.x: Screens for other causes: malignancy (weight loss, appetite, night sweats), viral hepatitis risks, cholestasis, NSAIDs/anticoagulants, epigastric, biliary and pancreatic pain — at least four areas.
check.d: Score if at least four of these areas are screened.

check.x: Past history, medicines and allergies: hypertension for 15 years and high cholesterol for 12 years, perindopril and simvastatin with poorer adherence this month, and no allergies.
Social history: never smoked, no drugs, lives alone with 2 dogs, children interstate, retired journalist.
Explores the bereavement and his mood (wife died a month ago, low mood, poor sleep).
Asks directly about thoughts of self-harm or suicide (none; "the dogs keep me going").
Explores his ideas, concerns and expectations: he links it to his drinking, is frightened by the blood and is worried about his dogs.
Examination

Assesses haemodynamic status: pallor, sweating, pulse, BP and capillary refill, and recognises resting tachycardia (HR 108) as significant blood loss; a sitting BP if done safely (100/64, HR 124, light-headed); conscious state.
check.d: Credit a sitting or postural BP if done safely, but do not require it: the resting tachycardia already shows significant volume loss.

check.x: Looks for the peripheral stigmata of chronic liver disease and identifies at least four (for example palmar erythema, leukonychia, forearm bruising, scleral icterus, proximal muscle wasting (thin arms), spider naevi, gynaecomastia).
check.d: Score if at least four stigmata are identified; the candidate does not need to name every one. Conjunctival pallor is a sign of anaemia from the bleed, not a stigma of chronic liver disease, and does not count towards the four.

check.x: Assesses for hepatic encephalopathy and alcohol withdrawal: orientation and attention, asterixis (absent) and tremor (fine tremor present).
Examines the abdomen:

kids.x: Inspection: distension, full flanks, caput medusae
Palpation: right upper quadrant tenderness (no guarding, Murphy's sign negative), a firm irregular liver edge 3 cm below the costal margin and a palpable spleen tip
Percussion: flank dullness and shifting dullness to confirm ascites

check.x: Requests a rectal examination for melaena (found) and examines for peripheral oedema (pitting to mid-shin).
Interpretation

Interprets the observations: after the further haematemesis at 08:45, HR 126 to 130 and systolic BP 94 to 92 are in the yellow zone (clinical review). With ongoing bleeding and a shock index above 1 he is in early haemorrhagic shock, so the candidate escalates to a senior doctor now, without waiting 30 minutes.

Interprets the bloods: Hb 92 falling to 84 (active bleeding, Hb lags), urea 11.8 with normal creatinine (upper GI source), platelets 82, bilirubin 48, albumin 27 and INR 1.8 (decompensated cirrhosis with portal hypertension), lactate 2.4 (hypoperfusion).
check.d: The critical element is recognising decompensated cirrhosis with impaired synthetic function (bilirubin, albumin, INR). Credit Child-Pugh C if stated, but do not require it.

check.x: Interprets the ultrasound: cirrhosis with splenomegaly and ascites (portal hypertension), no focal lesion.

Gives the most likely diagnosis as an acute upper GI bleed from oesophageal varices in decompensated alcohol-related cirrhosis, supported by heavy alcohol use, ascites, splenomegaly, stigmata of liver disease and impaired synthetic function.

Gives differentials with the feature for or against each: peptic ulcer (no NSAIDs or epigastric pain, but can coexist), Mallory-Weiss tear (no preceding retching), hepatocellular carcinoma (cirrhosis and pain, but no weight loss or focal lesion), cholecystitis (pain chronic and not colicky, normal gallbladder), chronic pancreatitis (no back pain or steatorrhoea, no pancreatic calcification seen on ultrasound).
check.d: Score if at least three appropriate differentials are given with a supporting or opposing feature, and peptic ulcer is one of them.

check.x: Management

Resuscitates: two large-bore cannulae, crossmatch, and transfuses red cells now while he is shocked and bleeding, guided by haemodynamics; restrictive transfusion (below about 70 g/L, target 70 to 80 g/L) once stable, to avoid raising portal pressure.
check.d: The critical element is giving blood to a shocked, actively bleeding patient guided by haemodynamics. Credit airway protection, cautious fluids and the massive transfusion protocol if mentioned, but do not require them.

check.x: Starts a vasoactive drug before endoscopy: terlipressin 2 mg IV 4-hourly, or octreotide 50 micrograms IV bolus then 50 micrograms/hour.
check.d: Either drug at a correct dose earns the mark. Checking an ECG for ischaemia before terlipressin is good practice and may be credited, but is not required.

check.x: Gives antibiotic prophylaxis for a GI bleed in cirrhosis: ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily.
Calls the gastroenterology registrar for urgent endoscopy with band ligation within 12 hours once resuscitated, admits him, and involves ICU or HDU if he stays unstable.

Gives IV thiamine with or before glucose (for example 300 mg IV; more if Wernicke encephalopathy is suspected) and starts alcohol withdrawal monitoring with symptom-triggered treatment on senior advice.
check.d: Essential: parenteral thiamine and withdrawal monitoring with treatment on senior advice. The exact thiamine dose, the named withdrawal scale and the choice of benzodiazepine (a shorter-acting one such as oxazepam or lorazepam in decompensated liver disease) are credited if given but not required.

check.x: Gives at least 2 supportive steps: nil by mouth, withholds perindopril, avoids NSAIDs, no routine FFP for the INR, an IV PPI until endoscopy, a diagnostic ascitic tap for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.

Explains to James in plain words, without judgement, that the drinking has scarred his liver and caused swollen veins in the food pipe that are bleeding; explains the camera test, the need to stay in hospital and the importance of stopping alcohol; checks understanding.
Addresses his practical worries and grief: any two of social work for the dogs, offering to contact his children, grief support, drug and alcohol team.
Safety netting

Asks the nurses to report at once at least 4 of: more blood vomited, black stools, feeling faint or a falling BP, new confusion or drowsiness, shakes, sweats or seeing things (withdrawal), fever, worsening tummy pain or swelling.
Mentions the longer-term plan (banding programme with a beta-blocker, liver cancer surveillance) at any point in Part 2.

part2.lead: Here are James's observations since arrival, including a repeat set after he vomited again, his blood results and venous gas, and the abdominal ultrasound report.
part2.patient:
When the examiner reads out your question for question 4 ("Is this because of my drinking? What happens now?"), react to how the candidate answers:

  • If the candidate is kind and non-judgemental, become tearful and say: "Margaret would be furious with me. I'll do whatever it takes."
  • If the candidate lectures you, go quiet and look away.
  • If the candidate has not mentioned the dogs, ask once: "Who will look after my dogs?"
  • If the candidate uses jargon (varices, endoscopy, cirrhosis), ask once: "What does that mean?"

handover.label: Observations since arrival
handover.result: On room air throughout. At 08:45 he vomited about 300 mL of fresh red blood with clots. Now pale and clammy, still alert and oriented.
handover.model:
• Read: on arrival (08:10) every value is in the white zone, but HR 108 with haematemesis and melaena already means he is compensating for blood loss. At 08:45, after a further 300 mL haematemesis, HR 126 and systolic BP 94 are both in the yellow zone. At 08:55, HR 130 and systolic 92 are still yellow and getting worse. RR, SpO2, temperature and consciousness are white.
  • Meaning: ongoing bleeding with early haemorrhagic shock. The shock index (HR divided by systolic BP) is about 1.4. A white zone on arrival did not make him safe. In a man treated for hypertension for 15 years, a systolic of 92 is well below his usual and more significant than the number alone suggests.
  • Changes: the yellow zone calls for a clinical review within 30 minutes. With active bleeding the candidate does not wait: senior ED doctor to the bedside now, gastroenterology and ICU early, a rapid response if systolic falls below 90 or any value turns red, and observations every 15 minutes.

rows.note: Triage: vomited blood at home. To acute bay, monitoring on
Vomited about 300 mL fresh blood with clots. Doctor informed
Repeat set: pale and clammy. Venous gas taken

handover.label: Bloods and venous gas
handover.result: Bloods collected 08:20 at cannulation; venous gas at 08:50, after the further haematemesis at 08:45. Hepatitis B and C serology, iron studies and alpha-fetoprotein sent, results to follow. No previous results on file.
handover.model:
• Read: Hb 92 g/L falling to 84 g/L on the gas half an hour later. Platelets 82. INR 1.8. Bilirubin 48, albumin 27. Urea 11.8 with a normal creatinine. Lactate 2.4 with a mildly low bicarbonate. Also MCV 104, AST 148 more than twice ALT 64, GGT 410, ALP mildly raised, sodium 131, lipase normal.
  • Meaning: active blood loss, and the Hb will keep falling as he bleeds and is given fluid. Raised urea with a normal creatinine fits digested blood from an upper GI source. Low platelets fit hypersplenism from portal hypertension. Bilirubin, albumin and INR show decompensated cirrhosis with impaired synthetic function; with moderate ascites and no encephalopathy the Child-Pugh score is 11 (class C), credited but not required. The lactate shows hypoperfusion. Macrocytosis, the AST:ALT pattern and the low sodium fit alcohol and cirrhosis (supporting detail, not scored). A normal lipase argues against acute pancreatitis (it does not exclude chronic pancreatitis). The Glasgow-Blatchford score is about 14 to 16 (depending on which BP is used), far above the level for outpatient care.
  • Changes: crossmatched blood available now; he is shocked and still bleeding, so transfuse according to haemodynamics and ongoing loss rather than waiting for the Hb to fall, and once stable use restrictive transfusion (transfuse below about 70 g/L, target 70 to 80 g/L). The INR reflects liver failure and is not routinely corrected with FFP. Watch sodium on terlipressin. Child-Pugh C means high risk of rebleeding and death, so involve gastroenterology now.

labs.title: Full blood count, coagulation and group (08:20)

handover.label: Abdominal ultrasound
handover.result:
Examination: ultrasound of the abdomen with Doppler of the portal vein; portable departmental ultrasound performed at the bedside by the radiology sonographer at 08:30, alongside resuscitation. It did not delay resuscitation or referral for endoscopy.

Clinical details: 62-year-old man, heavy alcohol use, right upper quadrant pain for 3 years and worse over 3 weeks, new abdominal distension, haematemesis this morning. ?Chronic liver disease ?Focal lesion ?Biliary disease.

Findings:

  • Liver: span 17 cm in the midclavicular line. Coarse, heterogeneous echotexture with a nodular surface, and hypertrophy of the caudate lobe. No focal liver lesion seen.
  • Portal vein: patent, diameter 14 mm, with hepatopetal flow at reduced velocity. No thrombus. Hepatic veins patent.
  • Spleen: enlarged at 15 cm, homogeneous.
  • Peritoneum: moderate volume of simple free fluid in all four quadrants, enough for paracentesis from the left iliac fossa.
  • Gallbladder and bile ducts: gallbladder wall not thickened (allowing for the ascites), no stones, no pericholecystic fluid, sonographic Murphy sign negative. Common bile duct 5 mm. No intrahepatic duct dilatation.
  • Pancreas: head and body appear normal with no calcification or duct dilatation; tail obscured by bowel gas.
  • Kidneys: normal size, no hydronephrosis.

Conclusion: cirrhotic liver morphology with features of portal hypertension (splenomegaly, moderate ascites, slow portal flow). Patent portal vein. No focal liver lesion. No gallstones or cholecystitis.
handover.model:
• Read: nodular surface, coarse echotexture and caudate hypertrophy (cirrhosis). Splenomegaly, moderate ascites and slow portal flow (portal hypertension). Patent portal vein. No focal lesion. Normal gallbladder and ducts. Visible pancreas normal.
  • Meaning: confirms cirrhosis with portal hypertension, which makes oesophageal varices the most likely bleeding source and explains the ascites and low platelets. No focal lesion makes hepatocellular carcinoma less likely but does not exclude it (AFP pending, and cirrhosis needs surveillance). A normal gallbladder argues against cholecystitis. No calcification argues against chronic pancreatitis.
  • Changes: supports vasoactive treatment, antibiotic prophylaxis and urgent endoscopy. New ascites with a GI bleed calls for a diagnostic tap to exclude spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. A patent portal vein matters if TIPS is considered.

ask: You are now calling the gastroenterology registrar. Please give an ISBAR handover of James Holloway, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of James now, here in the emergency department.
James asks you, "Is this because of my drinking? What happens now?" Please answer him, then tell me what you would ask the nurses to watch for.
expect:
• Identify: self, ED junior doctor; James Holloway, 62.
  • Situation: haematemesis twice at home and 300 mL more at 08:45, with melaena; now HR 130, BP 92/56 (yellow zone), suspected variceal bleed.
  • Background: about 15 years of heavy drinking, 15 standard drinks a day since his wife died a month ago, last drink 11 pm; 3 years of RUQ pain, 3 weeks of swelling; hypertension on perindopril; no NSAIDs or anticoagulants.
  • Assessment: Hb 92 falling to 84 = active bleeding; urea 11.8 with normal creatinine = upper GI source; bilirubin 48, albumin 27, INR 1.8, platelets 82 = decompensated cirrhosis, Child-Pugh C; lactate 2.4; ultrasound shows cirrhosis, splenomegaly and ascites, no focal lesion.
  • Recommendation: please review now for urgent endoscopy; I am starting terlipressin and ceftriaxone, crossmatching, and asking ICU to review.

Most likely: acute oesophageal variceal haemorrhage in decompensated alcohol-related cirrhosis. For it: heavy prolonged drinking, large-volume haematemesis without preceding retching or epigastric pain, melaena, ascites, splenomegaly, stigmata (spider naevi, palmar erythema, gynaecomastia, icterus), low platelets, INR 1.8, albumin 27, cirrhosis with portal hypertension on ultrasound.

  • Peptic ulcer: for: alcohol, upper GI bleed, can coexist in cirrhosis; against: no NSAIDs, no epigastric pain. Only endoscopy separates them.
  • Mallory-Weiss tear: against: no retching before the blood.
  • Hepatocellular carcinoma: for: cirrhosis, RUQ pain; against: no weight loss, no focal lesion; AFP pending.
  • Cholecystitis: against: chronic dull non-colicky pain, afebrile, normal gallbladder.
  • Chronic pancreatitis: against: no back pain, no steatorrhoea, no calcification on the visible pancreas; a normal lipase does not exclude it.

1. Resuscitate: senior to the bedside, two large-bore cannulae, crossmatch; transfuse now while shocked and bleeding, then restrictively (below about 70 g/L, target 70 to 80).
  2. Terlipressin 2 mg IV 4-hourly or octreotide 50 micrograms bolus then 50 micrograms/hour.
  3. Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily.
  4. Urgent gastroenterology: endoscopy with banding within 12 hours; ICU or HDU if unstable.
  5. IV thiamine with or before glucose; withdrawal monitoring with symptom-triggered treatment on senior advice.
  6. Nil by mouth, withhold perindopril, no NSAIDs, no routine FFP, IV PPI, diagnostic ascitic tap.

• Plain words, no judgement: yes, years of drinking have scarred the liver, and the pressure has made veins in the food pipe swell and bleed; it is serious but treatable; he needs a camera test today to band the veins and must stay in hospital; stopping alcohol completely is the most important thing for his liver; checks understanding.
  • What happens next: repeat banding sessions with a beta-blocker as the liver team advises, stopping alcohol, and a liver ultrasound every 6 months to check for cancer.
  • Practical worries and grief (any two): social work for the dogs, offer to contact his children, grief support, drug and alcohol team.
  • Nurses to report at once (at least 4): more blood vomited, black stools, faintness or a falling BP, new confusion or drowsiness, shakes, sweats or seeing things, fever, worsening tummy pain or swelling.

guide:
In Part 1, the patient answers the history, the nurse gives the observations when asked, and the examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they are examining. If the candidate orders treatment in Part 1, say "Noted, please cover it in Part 2". Mark the early instructions to the nurse under Professionalism. If the candidate asks for results, say they will come in Part 2. In Part 2, hand over the observations, bloods and ultrasound report, then ask the four questions in order. Read out James's question for the fourth.

Score the stigmata item when at least four are identified. Credit a sitting BP if done safely, but do not require it: the resting tachycardia is enough. In the bloods item the critical element is recognising decompensated cirrhosis with impaired synthetic function; credit Child-Pugh C but do not require it.

A high-performing candidate gets cannulae, bloods and a crossmatch going within the first minute and then takes a focused history. That history characterises the haematemesis (no preceding retching, melaena), quantifies the alcohol in standard drinks with the last drink, screens for malignancy, hepatitis, ulcer, biliary and pancreatic causes, and handles the bereavement with empathy. They examine for haemodynamic compromise (recognising the resting tachycardia; a sitting BP only if safe), the stigmata of chronic liver disease, asterixis, ascites by shifting dullness and melaena. In Part 2 they see the worsening yellow zone observations as early haemorrhagic shock and escalate at once. They read the bloods as decompensated cirrhosis with an upper GI bleed and give a variceal bleed as the diagnosis. Their management covers resuscitation with blood given to haemodynamics while he is shocked and bleeding, terlipressin or octreotide, ceftriaxone, urgent endoscopy and thiamine. They explain in plain words, tell the nurses what to watch for and briefly outline the longer-term plan.

A borderline candidate takes a long pain history before addressing the bleeding, records alcohol vaguely ("a social drinker"), does not examine for ascites or melaena, accepts white zone observations on arrival as reassuring, or treats it as a peptic ulcer with a PPI alone. They may withhold blood from a shocked patient because the Hb is above 70, transfuse to a normal Hb, correct the INR with FFP, leave out antibiotic prophylaxis or the vasoactive drug, or forget thiamine and withdrawal.
explain:
The diagnosis

James has large-volume haematemesis without preceding retching or epigastric pain, with melaena, on a background of 15 years of heavy drinking, recently much heavier during grief. He has chronic right upper quadrant pain, new ascites, splenomegaly and the stigmata of chronic liver disease. That makes an acute variceal bleed in decompensated alcohol-related cirrhosis the leading diagnosis. Ascites and varices are both signs of portal hypertension. Localising the pain matters: chronic dull right upper quadrant pain points to the liver rather than to an epigastric peptic ulcer, and a detailed social history is what moves alcohol-related liver disease to the top of the list.

Differentials

  • Peptic ulcer: common in heavy drinkers and in people with cirrhosis. Without endoscopy it cannot be excluded, which is why a PPI is often given until the gastroscopy.
  • Mallory-Weiss tear: typically follows forceful retching. James had none.
  • Portal hypertensive gastropathy: usually causes slower bleeding.
  • Hepatocellular carcinoma: may present with pain or decompensation in cirrhosis. Ask about weight loss, appetite, night sweats and fever, and arrange imaging and AFP.
  • Cholecystitis: less likely. Biliary pain is colicky, related to meals and acute rather than chronic and dull.
  • Chronic pancreatitis: worth considering with this much alcohol, but there is no epigastric pain radiating to the back, no steatorrhoea, no weight loss and no calcification on the visible pancreas. A normal lipase does not exclude it, because lipase is often normal in chronic pancreatitis.
  • Superimposed alcohol-related hepatitis: possible after a month of very heavy drinking. A bilirubin of 48, no fever and a normal white cell count make severe disease less likely.

Interpreting the results

White zone observations on arrival hid a compensating patient. After the next bleed his heart rate and systolic BP entered the yellow zone, which under NSW Between the Flags calls for a clinical review. With active bleeding and a shock index above 1, the right response is immediate senior escalation. The haemoglobin lags behind the bleed and falls as fluid is given. A raised urea with a normal creatinine reflects digested blood. Macrocytosis (MCV 104), AST more than twice ALT and a GGT of 410 fit alcohol. Sodium 131 fits cirrhosis with ascites and needs watching on terlipressin. A normal lipase argues against acute pancreatitis but does not exclude chronic pancreatitis. Thrombocytopenia reflects hypersplenism. Bilirubin 48, albumin 27, INR 1.8 and moderate ascites without encephalopathy give a Child-Pugh score of 11 (class C). The ultrasound confirms cirrhosis with portal hypertension, a patent portal vein and no focal lesion; it was done at the bedside alongside resuscitation, before the rebleed, and must never delay escalation or endoscopy. The Glasgow-Blatchford score is about 14 to 16 (depending on which BP is used), far above the low-risk level that allows outpatient care.

Management of a suspected variceal bleed

  • Resuscitation: ABC, two large-bore cannulae, crossmatch and senior help. Protect the airway (intubate) before endoscopy if bleeding is massive or consciousness is impaired. Give fluids cautiously and, in a haemodynamically stable patient, use a restrictive transfusion strategy, transfusing at a haemoglobin of about 70 g/L with a target of 70 to 80 g/L, because over-transfusion raises portal pressure and increases rebleeding. With ongoing bleeding and shock, transfuse according to haemodynamics and ongoing loss rather than waiting for the Hb to fall, with crossmatched blood available now. Activate the massive transfusion protocol for exsanguinating haemorrhage. Do not routinely correct the INR with FFP, because in cirrhosis it does not reflect bleeding risk well.
  • Vasoactive drug as soon as a variceal bleed is suspected, before endoscopy: terlipressin 2 mg IV 4-hourly, or octreotide 50 micrograms IV bolus then 50 micrograms/hour. Check for ischaemic heart disease (ECG) before terlipressin, and monitor sodium.
  • Antibiotic prophylaxis: ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily, which reduces infection, rebleeding and death in cirrhosis with a GI bleed.
  • Urgent endoscopy within 12 hours once resuscitated, with band ligation of oesophageal varices. IV erythromycin before endoscopy can improve the view. For Child-Pugh C (10 to 13), Baveno VII advises considering pre-emptive TIPS within 72 hours. Uncontrolled bleeding is bridged with balloon tamponade or an oesophageal stent while TIPS is arranged.
  • Other: nil by mouth, withhold the ACE inhibitor, avoid NSAIDs and sedatives where possible, and do a diagnostic ascitic tap to exclude spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. Watch for hepatic encephalopathy, because a GI bleed is a common trigger.

Alcohol withdrawal and thiamine

His last drink was at 11 pm, so withdrawal can begin within hours, with seizures most likely in the first 2 days and delirium tremens after that. His tachycardia and fine tremor may partly reflect early withdrawal as well as blood loss. Give parenteral thiamine with or before glucose (never delay glucose for hypoglycaemia) to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy: thiamine 300 mg IV daily (higher doses, e.g. 500 mg IV three times daily, if Wernicke encephalopathy is suspected). Monitor with an alcohol withdrawal scale. In decompensated cirrhosis a shorter-acting benzodiazepine such as oxazepam or lorazepam (oral doses with sips of water are acceptable while nil by mouth; if oral is not possible, a parenteral benzodiazepine on senior or ICU advice) is preferred, symptom-triggered, with senior advice, because oversedation can mimic or precipitate encephalopathy.

The person behind the bleed

His drinking escalated after his wife's death. He needs non-judgemental care, a mood and risk assessment, grief support, social work (including care for his dogs) and the drug and alcohol team. Medicines to prevent relapse are chosen with specialist advice, because several are unsafe in advanced liver disease.

Safety netting and follow-up

In hospital, the nurses and James report more haematemesis, black stools, faintness, confusion, withdrawal symptoms or fever straight away. Later, before discharge (not scored in this station), he is told to call 000 for vomiting blood or collapse and to come to the ED for black stools, confusion, or fever with abdominal pain. Follow-up covers a banding programme with a non-selective beta-blocker as the gastroenterologists advise, 6-monthly ultrasound surveillance for hepatocellular carcinoma, the hepatitis serology results, abstinence support and GP review within a week.
points: In a heavy drinker with haematemesis, ascites and stigmata of chronic liver disease, treat the bleed as variceal until endoscopy proves otherwise.
White zone observations on arrival do not exclude significant blood loss. A rising heart rate and falling BP after a further bleed mean early haemorrhagic shock and need immediate senior escalation.
Start a vasoactive drug (terlipressin 2 mg IV 4-hourly or octreotide) and ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily before endoscopy, and arrange endoscopy with band ligation within 12 hours.

Transfuse restrictively in a haemodynamically stable patient (at a haemoglobin of about 70 g/L, target 70 to 80 g/L), because over-transfusion raises portal pressure; do not routinely correct the INR with FFP.
Bilirubin, albumin, INR, ascites and encephalopathy make up the Child-Pugh score; Child-Pugh C after a variceal bleed carries a high risk of rebleeding and death.

Quantify alcohol in standard drinks with the time of the last drink, give parenteral thiamine with or before glucose (never delay glucose for hypoglycaemia), monitor for withdrawal, and address the grief that drove the drinking.

ddx.dx: Acute oesophageal variceal haemorrhage in decompensated alcohol-related cirrhosis
ddx.for: Fifteen years of heavy drinking, large-volume haematemesis with melaena, ascites, splenomegaly, stigmata of chronic liver disease, platelets 82, INR 1.8, albumin 27 and cirrhosis with portal hypertension on ultrasound.
Heavy alcohol use and an upper GI bleed with melaena and a raised urea, and an ulcer can coexist with cirrhosis.
ddx.against: No NSAIDs, no epigastric pain or indigestion, and only endoscopy can tell the two apart.
The blood came up without any retching or vomiting beforehand.

ddx.for: Cirrhosis with right upper quadrant pain that has worsened over 3 weeks and a firm, irregular liver edge.
ddx.against: No weight loss, night sweats or fever and no focal liver lesion on ultrasound, with the AFP still pending.

ddx.for: Right upper quadrant pain and tenderness.
ddx.against: The pain is chronic, dull and not colicky or related to meals, he is afebrile, Murphy's sign is negative and the gallbladder is normal on ultrasound.

ddx.for: Prolonged heavy alcohol use with upper abdominal pain.
ddx.against: No epigastric pain going through to the back, no steatorrhoea and no calcification in the visible pancreas, though a normal lipase does not exclude it.
